When the committee was last sitting on this item, on Friday, May 11, we were considering the item appearing at page 269 of the book of estimates, civil salaries and wages, $3,489,842. Some hon. members asked for a break-down of this item so as to present the information in the same form as for other departments of the government. At that time I indicated that the information was not readily available in that form. These details were not put in our estimates, at the direction of the treasury board itself, for the reason, I understand, that the growth in the department was so great that any information given would be out of date and not very useful for the purposes of giving consideration to these estimates.
As to the usefulness or otherwise of the information, I think hon. members can judge for themselves when they receive the information which I now give them. As I pointed out at the time, when I was asked for this it took some time to secure the information. I was not aware, at the time I said that, just how much work would be required. The work was started the next day, Saturday, May 12, and the employees worked' over both week ends, but only this afternoon did I receive the information, and it is now here on the same basis as for other government departments. It covers a total of 28,154 civilian employees of the department. In a month or two it will be 30,000. Before the end of the year it will probably be 35,000.
To obtain this information it was necessary to run through the cards of all civilian employees in the department and then sort them out by classifications and wage groupings. Altogether a total of fourteen personnel were involved in the task for two weeks and over Saturdays and Sundays.
The information was asked for, and here it is. It was not possible before today to have it mimeographed or printed. I do not think it would be desirable or useful to have it done. If hon. members so desire, it might be printed as an appendix to Hansard, or in the Votes and Proceedings, but I would be the last person in the house to suggest that that be done, or to object if anyone wants it done.
This is not a static department. Since September the development in defence operation, measured in terms of money, has been,

I believe, greater than at any period of corresponding length during the second world war. Perhaps this may be brought home by recalling that during the fiscal year 1939-40 the defence expenditures were $125,679,888, whereas during the following year, 1940-41, they were $647,922,940. But the appropriations voted by parliament for the current fiscal year, 1950-51, which was still in effect when the special session was held last August, amounted to $425 million. Now, as I have
Supply-National Defence informed hon. members, there is available out of the money voted last year, and in the consolidated revenue fund for this year or sought by these estimates for the year 1951-52, a total of $1,879 million.
The change is made plain by considering the number of service and civilian personnel in each of the last four years. Perhaps I might put this short table on Hansard. I will give it to hon. members, though I think it ought to go on in tabular form. It is as follows:

Hon. members can see that the figures disclosed for other government departments which are relatively static, showing the number of civil servants in each classification, the salary range and the total for each, is very useful information indeed; but in the case of this department at this time it is of no more use than it would have been during any year of the second world war, when, so far as I know, such information was neither sought nor given. I should like to indicate in a word or two the policy with regard to the employment of civilian personnel in the Department of National Defence. We find it very difficult indeed to estimate, with close accuracy, the number of civilians we shall be able to engage this year, or the number that will be needed. I suppose that will depend upon circumstances entirely outside the control of the department. This year we shall be working on the re-establishment of seven major air stations, and the creation of a large gunnery range on the northern boundary of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and in addition will be increasing the size, accommodation and operations of a large number of units. How much we can do will depend, in part, 86709-2131
upon what equipment we can obtain from the United States, upon events in Korea, and upon the rate of construction made possible by the supply of materials, labour and engineering plans. Upon these results will depend the number of civilian personnel we can usefully employ during the current fiscal year.
Our policy is to employ civilians in every position in which civilians could be properly employed in the event of war. That is, it is our policy to use just as small a number of service personnel as is possible on what may be called civilian occupations. I believe that, compared with other countries, we have succeeded in working that out to good advantage. Our proportion of service to civilian personnel is not far from what it is in the United Kingdom or the United States.

The second reason, however, is more important, and that is that we want just as large a proportion as possible of our service personnel to be engaged in training and operational duties, and we want to have as large a proportion as possible of service personnel-men, and now women-who are trained and physically fit and of an age suitable to perform duties appropriate to their rank and job throughout the first year of a general war.
This policy has enabled the Canadian forces, navy, army and air force, to be operational to at least as great as if not a greater extent than is found in most other countries, and yet at the same time to maintain the essential services, including communications, training and reserve units and so on, necessary in a country of this size, and to provide the basis for a maximum potential in the event of a general war.

On that occasion and at other times previously I pointed out that there was considerable agitation to have something done about housing. I noted a little while ago that something like $2 million is to be spent at Rockclifie to provide housing accommodation. If Wainwright is to be a permanent camp, something should be done. I should like to know what has been done up to the present time and what is contemplated for the near future.

I suggest that this question might properly come under the head of army on page 271, but since the hon. member asked it in the general discussion and I omitted to answer, perhaps I might do so now. It was not our intention to have Wainwright an all year round training camp. For one thing, and I say this with all respect to the hon. member, it is one of the coldest places in Canada. During Exercise Sweetbriar the temperature went to 58 below and the troops were living out in tents. It has a considerable snowfall as well.
It is an exceedingly good training area during the summer, and it was our intention to use it as a summer training camp for the active and reserve forces. To that end it was intended to make only a limited number of permanent improvements. It was intended also to have a limited amount of Arctic and sub-Arctic winter training done during the winter months for which we would not want married quarters. However, our intention, with regard to this camp has changed. It will be necessary to provide accommodation there for a larger number of men. In the first place, we plan to make it a camp which will be suitable for occupation by 5,000 officers and men, about a brigade group, and perhaps later to develop it further. It is the largest single training area we have in Canada with a very suitable terrain for training in summer, but unsuitable for general training in winter. It has 125,000 acres, or about 600 square miles. At the present time, therefore, our program does not include any provision for married quarters there, but in view of the development in our plans which has come about in the last few weeks or months we are reconsidering the situation as to married quarters, not only at Wainwright but also at other camps of a similar type that are being or will be established at places like Gimli, Portage la Prairie, Macdonald, Clares-holm, and of course the big area at Lac la Biche, as well as at Penhold. All that is being re-examined in the light of further developments.

speechtext: Yes, but somebody has to send submissions and contact the men of the Canadian Commercial Corporation; also the department decides what it should do and then asks the Canadian Commercial Corporation or Defence Construction Limited to do the job for us on our instructions. But we have quite a considerable staff, both in the department and in the services, engaged in deciding where we shall go, what we shall do, looking after inspections to a certain extent, and also of course supervising the design of buildings.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: The minister means that this Mr. Campbell is to some extent an architect, or carries on work of that kind?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: No. As far as I recall he was a former official of the Canadian Bank of Commerce engaged in construction, and since the war has been engaged in this operation for the department. He is, I think, considered, and very rightly so, highly skilled in matters of real estate, construction, planning and the like. He looked after this for the Canadian Bank of Commerce, I understand, and has had a great deal to do with this work in the department. That is a very large part in the department's operation.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: What is his salary at the present time without this terminable allowance?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: What is this terminable allowance? Why is he to be paid that?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: The reason for that is that his work is considered to be a very great responsibility, and a job that really justified a higher rate than this. The decision was that it should not be a rate above that of an assistant deputy minister, for which the current salary is $8,000. However, in view of the magnitude of the operations, the amount involved, and the great skill shown in handling them by Mr. Campbell it was established that he should require an additional allowance of $800 terminable on his ceasing to fill that appointment.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Does the minister mean by that that he will continue to get this extra $1,400 every year above the salary of $8,000?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
No; this $8,000 includes the terminable allowance. It was $6,600 salary plus $1,400 terminable allowance. They have

now been consolidated into a salary of $8,000, which is the same salary as that of an assistant deputy minister.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
I understand the minister,
in the course of the statement he made earlier, indicated that in the inspection service under this item there are 727 persons employed. I should like information on the item. First of all, are they all civilian personnel, and will the minister indicate the particular type of inspection service they render?
May I say in connection with that subject that this, I suggest, will call upon the minister for some indication of the way in which this inspection service is carried out vis-a vis the inspection service rendered previously by Canadian Commercial Corporation and now, under the new set-up of the Department of Defence Production, by Defence Construction Limited. Are any of those persons engaged in the inspection service in connection with the acquisition of property? Does their inspection extend that widely, and what is their relationship to the inspection service carried on by those charged with the negotiation of contracts, and the acquisition of properties or supplies under those contracts?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
The employees of the inspection service listed here are all civilians. They inspect all equipment of every kind purchased for the department, or the armed services, which requires inspection-except in a few and rather limited number of cases where an outside inspection firm is hired. They have to do with the inspection of ships, aircraft, armament, ammunition, food, clothing, barrack-room stores and everything else used by the armed forces.
With regard to their relationship to Canadian Commercial Corporation, while they work closely with that organization

or with Defence Construction Limited-they do not duplicate any of the work being done. The inspection of construction by architects or engineers is done by architects or engineers engaged by Canadian Commercial Corporation or Defence Construction Limited, but -acceptable to this department, reporting directly to it, and working very closely with it.
In the case of operational buildings inspection is done by members of the armed forces themselves. In addition to the civilian personnel to which I have referred, a considerable number of service personnel are engaged in inspection. Our effort is to integrate the two, so that they will be kept in line with each other. We hope to increase that so that we will have service personnel, who represent the user, working closely with civilian personnel in the inspection service. I should

like to add, as I said two weeks ago, that the inspection of equipment is carried out at every stage, so that at a plant such as that of the A. V. Roe Company there will be a large number of inspectors inspecting every part of each plane as it is made.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
I take it then that it is clear
that none of the 727 persons referred to is engaged in any respect in connection with the inspection of properties or defence projects. They are all on other forms of equipment or supplies; is that correct?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
They would be involved in
the inspection of materials entering into construction which was undertaken by a department of the services themselves. We would ordinarily employ architects or outside engineers, through Canadian Commercial Corporation and Defence Construction Limited, to inspect finished properties.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
There is a point in that connection that is not entirely clear. The minister has indicated that these 727 persons are all civilians. We are aware of the fact, of course, that some of the military personnel in the department do carry out the inspection of construction, and give their approval before a construction project is finally assumed by the department. In other cases professional persons or firms outside the department are engaged for the purpose of supervising and checking construction projects. But I understood from the minister's earlier statement that the kind of inspection that was carried out by the department was carried out exclusively by military personnel. I had taken from his earlier answer that none of the 727 persons has anything to do with the inspection of properties-that is to say, construction projects and properties. The minister's last answer leaves me in doubt as to whether that is the situation.
A considerable number of these 727 apparently are engaged in the inspection of equipment and materials coming in. Then he went on to speak about materials entering into construction projects.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
I went on to speak about materials entering into construction projects undertaken by the armed services, or the department itself. There are a limited number of construction projects, and that number is becoming fewer and fewer, in which we do a job of adding to a building here or there, without letting it out as a contract. In those cases the materials and construction would be inspected either by service personnel or by a member of our inspection service. We would not go out and, in addition, hire an architect or a contractor through Canadian Commercial Corporation to make that inspection.
Supply-National Defence

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Then, one other point, which is suggested by a reference made in another place. Has there been any change within the last year or two in the method of carrying out this inspection service, either with reference to construction projects on the one hand or the inspection of supplies and materials on the other?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I would have to make an inquiry to ascertain that. There must be changes every day in the technique and operation of inspection, particularly as the type of equipment is changing. For example we are now making a three-inch 50-calibre naval gun, requiring a large number of inspections. But that work is supplemented at Sorel Industries Limited by inspection made by United States naval personnel. How much they co-operate and how they interchange their information, I do not know but I can find out. There must be many developments of that kind.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: That is not the point; it is a question of some change within the last year or so in inspection procedure, or the method followed in the department in reference to inspection. The point is as to whether that has any bearing upon the respective functions of the Department of National Defence on the one hand and Canadian Commercial Corporation or the Department of Defence Production on the other.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member has not made his inquiry sufficiently clear to enable me to understand what he is getting at, or what information he wants to have.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Information in regard to the inspection procedure now obtaining either in the minister's department, on the one hand, or, on the other hand, the Department of Defence Production, Defence Construction Limited, or its predecessor, Canadian Commercial Corporation.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
I should think that there
would be steady development in the practice. I do not know personally of any major change in procedure and none has come to my attention or to the attention of the officers before me. I shall make inquiries, however.
Then with regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Broadview, I recognize that I was in error and I am sorry to have made the error. The reason for making it was that Mr. Dumsday was appointed to his position at a salary range of $6,000 to $6,600. The official before me, speaking from memory, told me that he was at the minimum of the salary range, or $6,000. Instead
3348	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence he was appointed at the maximum of his range, or $6,600. When the general increase for civil servants was passed his classification was increased to $6,180-$6,780, and Mr. Dumsday's salary was increased to that maximum. His increase in consequence of the general increase was only $180.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
I should
like to ask a question following that of the hon. member for Eglinton in connection with inspection and the sharing of duties of inspection. I am rather troubled by the number of agencies engaged in this work. I am rather reminded of the old rhyme:
Larger fleas have smaller fleas Upon their backs to bite 'em;
And these again have other fleas And so ad infinitum.
I do not minimize the importance of inspection because I realize it is a most serious matter. First we have national defence with its inspectors-I notice that the minister has said that he is hoping to increase the number of service personnel working on inspection along with the civilian personnel-then we have Canadian Commercial Corporation, although I understand that their status is to be reduced somewhat. Then we have defence production and defence construction, and then Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation acting as special advisers. It is almost inevitable when you have so many agencies employed at the one task that duplication occurs.
We had some rather frank and clear statements from the officials in the public accounts committee as to what the practice used to be. We are not allowed to come up to date in the public accounts committee. Would the minister indicate, first, whether he is satisfied that these duties are well apportioned and, second, if there has been any overlapping?
Take the case where the defence department orders aeroplanes. I understand that first they would determine what they want. Then they pass that information on to some other agency, I suppose defence production. Then they would have to follow it through to see that they get what they want as to both specification and quality. The Minister of Defence Production told us the other day that that department plays a part in this matter, and I should like to quote his statement, as reported on page 3099 of Hansard of May 16:
The engineering staff of defence production is small, but engineering services available to Defence Construction Limited are retained for the purpose of inspecting construction.
My understanding is that that refers exactly to what the minister said, to various
[Mr. Claxton.)

types of construction and not to munitions of war. I come back to my question and ask the minister to indicate the division of duties among these agencies. I cannot say that it is too clear, but I should like to know whether the minister is satisfied with what they are doing. Let us take the question of aeroplanes. Will he indicate the division of the functions of the Department of National Defence, defence production and its ancillary companies?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
I should like to ask the hon. member who has just expressed these vague fears if he knows of any reason for having them. If he knows of any failure of the services engaged in inspection to do their job properly I should like to hear about it. I have not heard about it and therefore I can assure him that I know of no reason for expressing dissatisfaction with the present situation. I hear of all cases that involve trouble, and I have heard of no case.
The hon. member asks me if I am satisfied. I am never satisfied with anything because I believe that everything can be improved. But we like to have constructive proposals upon which we can base improvement. This situation has been explained twice already, and I think again in the public accounts committee, but I shall try to do it again. There is no confusion.
The inspection services, acting for the Department of National Defence and the three armed services, navy, army and air force, either themselves or by means of outside inspectors in a small number of cases who are engaged because they have special experience and facilities and equipment which we have not-for example, in road building-inspect everything that we buy that requires inspection. That is, almost everything.
With regard to construction, that is done by architects or engineers engaged by Canadian Commercial Corporation or Defence Construction Limited, but with our recommendation of the persons involved. But at almost every stage on important undertaking, there are service personnel involved also.
Let us trace an order for aircraft from the beginning to the end. In the case of the F-86E we negotiated with the United States government for the acquisition of the right to make the aircraft in Canada. Air force experts were sent down to the North American Aviation Company plant at Los Angeles where they studied the production of the aircraft. They were joined by representatives of Canadair Limited who also studied the production of the aircraft. They

then brought back to Canada not only plans and blueprints but jigs and dies and perhaps the special inspection instruments required.
Then construction was started at Canadair Limited. Throughout the whole operation representatives of the armed forces would be present in three or four capacities, one being that of inspection. There would also be civilian inspectors who would inspect every part as it is made. Then finally the armed forces, with such civilian assistance of the inspection services as they may require, would inspect and flight-test the performance of the finished product. This works the same as it does in other countries. It applies the principle of inspection by the consumer for the consumer, and we think it is a good arrangement. If anyone suggests any improvement we will be very glad indeed to consider it.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Since the minister has raised the question of examination of aircraft as an example of the inspection service mentioned, would he take this opportunity to deal with a question that was asked earlier as reported at pages 3027 and 3028 of Hansard? It has to do with a press report of May 15 that approximately 1,000 planes are to be borrowed from the United States. Since this would tie in with the question of inspection, I would think it would be appropriate to explain how this is being handled, what inspection methods are being devised, and what the actual number of aircraft is that is being brought in in this way.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I think it would be a good thing to deal with civil salaries and wages at this time.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: It is interesting how quickly the minister decides that we should only deal with salaries and wages after he has just used as an illustration the inspection of aircraft. Since he has dealt with inspection of aircraft, I suggest it would be appropriate that he explain whether the same inspection groups will deal with the inspection of the aircraft that are being brought in, and which for obvious reasons would require perhaps an even more exacting type of inspection.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
The question of the leader of the opposition extended far beyond the realm of inspection. In the first instance he asked about the whole deal, but I do not mind when I answer these things, and I will try to do my best. But I do think it is a good thing to proceed in an orderly way. With respect to this matter, these aircraft do not number
1,000	but 100. They are borrowed from the United States. They are the T-6, which is the Harvard with modifications. They are
Supply-National Defence being delivered at Trenton by the United States air force, and are in good working condition. Any inspection that is done on them is done by service personnel, and is largely in the nature of test by flight. These aircraft are aircraft with which we are very familiar.
At the end of the year we will return to the United States 100 equivalent aircraft, and whatever inspection arrangements are provided with regard to one lot of aircraft will apply equally to the other. We will get from the United States aircraft in good working condition. We will return to them aircraft in good working condition. The operation has just started. I have not had brought to my attention details of inspection in addition to anything I have said. If it is desired I can get it.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: What are the qualifications for these civilian inspectors? I am particularly interested in four categories of manufacture: guns, small arms, aircraft and motor vehicles. I should like to know what kind of qualifications a man has to have before he can be an inspector employed by the Department of National Defence to inspect in plants manufacturing these various articles of war, and also what kind of salaries are paid to those performing these various services?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
The appointments are all made by the civil service commission in accordance with classifications that have been established by them. They were worked out during the war in connection with the joint inspection board, and have been changed from time to time since. Of course they are also in accordance with the views of our department. The salary ranges vary. They are scattered all the way through. For example, for an engineer grade 1 the range is $2,700 to $3,240; engineer grade 2, $2,976 to $3,888; engineer grade 3, $3,888 to $4,524; engineer grade 4, $4,272 to $4,896. Then there is inspector grade 1, $4,584 to $5,208; inspector of stores grade 1, $2,064 to $2,496; grade 2, $2,568 to $2,904; grade 3, $2,976 to $3,444; grade 4, $3,444 to $3,888.
Then there is technical officer, grade 2, $2,904	to	$3,576;	technical	officer	grade	3,$3,576	to	$4,212;	technical	officer	grade	4,$3,888	to	$4,524;	technical	officer	grade	5,$4,272	to	$4,896.	Then there is technician,
grade 1, $2,772 to $3,028; grade 2, $2,904 to $3,240; grade 3, $3,240 to $3,576; grade 4, $3,576 to $3,888.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
What kind of inspection staff would we have at the gun plant at Sorel inspecting the manufacture, for example, of the 3-inch naval guns that have been mentioned? What kind of personnel would be there making sure we get the right kind of guns?

Supply-National Defence

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: We have largely armament inspectors who have qualified in work of that kind during the war and in Canadian Arsenals Limited since, and are of the type of official mentioned here. Some of them inspect each item in the equipment as it is made. I would estimate that there are between fifty and one hundred inspectors at Sorel Industries at the present time.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: All civilian?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: In addition to members of the navy as well.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Earlier the minister indicated the department's intention to utilize civilian personnel as far as possible, thus freeing service personnel for the duties for which they were enlisted. Would the minister indicate how far that policy will go? In the actual operation of an air station such as Penhold, to what extent would you utilize civilian personnel?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: There we would utilize civilian personnel in works services, that is, maintenance work, painting, ground keeping, road keeping and the like. As civilian guards we would use either the corps of commissionaires or other guards. In the kitchen services they would be used as assistant cooks, waiters, dish washers, and in work of that kind.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I should like to point out to the minister that I agree wholeheartedly with this policy. What about the age restriction? I recall that during the last war many of our older people found employment at Bowden under civilian administration and to a limited extent at Penhold. They were persons who could not fit into industry but were quite capable of doing the types of work mentioned by the minister. Is an age restriction to be imposed, or have you gone that far in your plan?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
It is entirely governed by
the civil service rules. Some of these employees may be temporary civil servants and others will be prevailing rate employees. Both classes will be governed by the civil service rules.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
Would the minister know
whether or not that was the case during the last war?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I am informed that at Pen-hold at that time the operations were carried on by a private company.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I think that was Bowden, was it not?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
Bowden. It acted as a contractor for the department, and engaged personnel itself. We have that kind of arrangement at the present time for catering

for summer camps. We pay the caterer so much a day, give him the food, and he supplies the staff which he hires.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Does the department contemplate having any of these fields operate on a similar basis, namely, administered by a civilian organization? I think it was the Edmonton flying club that administered Bowden. Is there any intention of following the same policy again?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Not at the major air training stations.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: May I ask to what extent women are employed as cooks and so on, and whether the department has under consideration the possibility of using more women in different capacities in order to release men for active service.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Yes, indeed.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Then with respect to the service schools in which the children of service personnel are educated at various points across the country, do those teachers come under this item of civil salaries and wages, and are those teachers service men and women or are they civilians?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: The teachers in the schools operated by the department for the children of service personnel are civilians. They do not come under this heading; they come under the heading of civilian employees in each of the services, navy, army and air force. Incidentally, they are usually engaged in co-operation with the provincial school authorities and have to be qualified according to the regulations of the province in which they are employed.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I had intended to ask whether there was a connection with the provincial authorities.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Yes, there is; and the schools are inspected by the provincial authorities. We meet local provincial standards, and indeed in most of the provinces we work, by arrangement with the provincial authorities, in exactly the same way a municipal school organization would. For example, the school at Barriefield will have a school board created and operated exactly the same as a school board would operate in an adjacent civilian municipality, with the same number of members on the board, the same titles, the same functions and the same responsibilities.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Do the members of these school boards receive any compensation for the services they render?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: None at all.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Then there is no charge against this department for inspection service or anything of that nature with regard to the schools?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Does Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have anything to do with the construction of homes on R.C.A.F. stations?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
Central Mortgage and
Housing built a very large proportion of the homes for us until two or three months ago, when that operation was taken over by Defence Construction Limited. C.M.H.C. are still carrying on with a very considerable number of homes that are unfinished.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Following that up, no doubt Central Mortgage and Housing have their inspectors looking over these houses from time to time. Does the air force also maintain an inspection staff for this purpose?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Not specifically, but the air officers in charge of works co-operate closely, and if they are not satisfied with the type of construction they report that fact and it is brought to the attention of Central Mortgage and Housing.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: I wonder if the minister is in a position to say what plans the department has, if any, for the use or expansion of the Grande Prairie airport. Is it proposed to make any extensive use of it in the defence of the great northwest?

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Like all other airports in existence Grande Prairie of course is under consideration in the event of any future development, but there is nothing in mind at the present time.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext:
Of course the minister understands the importance of that airport in connection with the threat to the northwest. I was also wondering whether any negotiations have been carried on with a view to having the United States share with the dominion and provincial governments the cost of building a communications link, which no doubt would be a road, between Fort St. John, let us say, which is the end of the Alaska highway, and the industrial centres of the middle western United States. That would entail quite a construction program over the area between Edmonton and Fort St. John, of course. I understand the provincial government is going ahead with a survey between Edmonton and Valley view, if I remember correctly, which is very close to Grande Prairie. I wonder if any thought has been given to asking the United States to share in the cost of that road.
Supply-National Defence

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: We have had representations from the chamber of commerce of Edmonton and other bodies that we should undertake this job as a defence project. We have considered it, and have decided that it is not so very different from fifty other proposals that have been made that the federal government should assist in the development of transportation facilities which it is true would be an advantage in the event of war but which we feel would be of far greater civilian advantage. These matters are always under consideration, but so far we have not decided to do anything in the case mentioned by the hon. member. With regard to the United States participation in it, under our arrangements with the United States we have assumed responsibility for maintenance for the northwest highways in Canada. That seems quite a proper contribution by Canada to joint defence. While we do not exclude the possibility of United States assistance in the development of transportation facilities in peacetime, there would have to be a very positive and immediate advantage to the United States to justify us in contemplating any such request. Our present opinion is that if things of that kind are to be done at all they should be done by Canada.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: There is, of course, this particular reason why the United States should be brought in to share the cost of that link between Edmonton and Fort St. John. Today, as for many years past, great truck trains carrying tons of materials pass over the Alberta highway from Montana, through the Crowsnest pass and up into that country. These materials are necessary both for defence purposes and for the maintenance of United States posts. I would think it proper that they should be asked to share in the cost of maintaining and/or rebuilding those highways, because they are cutting them to pieces and the provincial government has to pay the cost of rebuilding them. During the last war when it was thought Alaska was in danger the United States found it greatly to its advantage to have some form of highway up into that country. They did build from Fort St. John away north into the Yukon and Alaska, but there was no link between Fort St. John and the industrial centres of southern Alberta and the United States. It seems to me this is the time to be negotiating for the completion of that highway so that if and when trouble arises it will be there and the United States will have contributed at least its share to the cost of construction, because certainly they will be using it.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: Another matter I think is of importance is the replacement of serving staffs, cooks and so on, by civilians. I know that at Petawawa camp, where I have gone for several summers, the catering has been by civilians, and it has been done to the great satisfaction of all military personnel. I wonder to what extent that has become general or is going to become general? It seems to me that the practice of using army personnel for cooks or waiters is waste, and that is a good plan. I wonder if it is going to be general.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-SUGGESTED PLACING OF FLAGS IN MEMORIAL CHAMBER
speechtext: For the army, my recollection is that we made contracts with twelve contractors, and that those contracts are still in force. They supply the services-we supply the food-at charges which vary with the locality, the facilities and the number of meals served. The cost is approximately forty cents to sixty-five cents per day. The satisfaction depends on both the skill of the caterer and the direction he has been able to give to his own staff, and also the co-operation and services of the messing officer or dietitian of the armed forces on the spot. Where they have worked well together, it has gone very well. It is our intention to continue to do this in the places where we have exceptional peak loads, such as Petawawa, Valcartier and so on where summer training is done. In establishments where we have to have messing done on a fairly full level all the year round, our practice is to have service cooks and their immediate assistants who belong to one of the services; the subordinate job is done by civilians. We do this in order to build up as large a reservoir as we possibly can of trained and good cooks. During the last three years we have had considerable success in attracting more men into cooking branches and also through training courses. I think the standard has improved.

I pointed out that the most convenient way that this could be presented was to present it in the same way that it is presented to the members of the House of Commons in Great Britain. To give them in addition in the form followed by the armed forces in Britain would require that our figures, books and cards be kept in a different way. If that is the desire we can keep them in a different way. that you cannot get your eye on the pea, that you have got to guess. It is the old sleight of hand question, and you can never locate the pea. In sitting and listening to the debate, it has been most difficult to extract the information which some hon. members believe he is entitled to, and which I am sure he is entitled to. After a great deal of argument it finally comes to light that the information was sitting on the desk of the minister across the house, and it was not divulged to the person seeking it.
The minister's department probably has
30,000	employees. The situation is probably not due to his fault but because of the general scheme and plan of keeping records in his department. I am sure that every department probably has the same jumbled up mess. Take a corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway with 60,000 employees on pension and salary. I believe that if an executive in the head office of the C.P.R. in Montreal asked a question regarding a man's salary that information could be located in five minutes.

The minister spoke about increasing the staff but it is almost impossible to keep your finger on the pea or to secure the information. We are going to have an increase of 5,000. I hope that the war situation does not get much worse, so that the department will have to administer an army of 700,000. We would not know whether we were paying Chinese communists or Russians. We would not know who was on our payroll if we ever had an army of 700,000. We have a comparatively small army. The chiefs of staff, their staffs, and other civil servants apparently find it most difficult to be able to give the Minister of National Defence information that is available at any time in any well run corporation. It certainly is not available in the minister's department.
I am not saying that is his fault, but I do suggest that apparently a change is necessary. Efficiency should be department, so that in future he will not be placed in the embarrassing position of having
Supply-National Defence to tell the members of this house that he cannot give information which I believe should be available almost instantaneously. He should have a proper list of employees, with their salaries, their ages and where they are located.
I bring to the attention of the committee the example of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has 60,000 employees. I remember that while travelling on that railway some years ago the engine ran into some difficulty. When I reached Montreal I visited the office of the administrator of rolling stock and remarked that this engine, giving the number, had run into this difficulty which delayed the arrival of the train by some hours. The man in charge of rolling stock at that time pressed a button and called for the history of that engine; and there it was in full detail. He showed me the fuel consumption of the engine since it had been placed in service, the number of miles it had travelled, the number of times it had been repaired and so on. He assured me that applied to every single piece of rolling stock on that railway; he had all that information right under his thumb. I believe the Canadian Pacific has as many pieces of rolling stock as we have in the army, and on the railway they travel more frequently and more rapidly than is the case with our armed forces; yet the man in charge of that department could tell any visitor the cost of any piece of equipment, the cost of its operation and so on, by pressing a button and calling for a number.
Surely some similar method, or something almost as good, should be introduced to keep track of the employees of this government, whether they be members of the armed forces of whether they be on the civilian staffs of those forces. This discussion today has been most enlightening in that it has brought out; the lack of system and lack of efficiency in this particular department. As I say, I am not blaming the minister. Very often a man is placed in a department and has to carry on for years under, the set-up that was there long before he got there; but we certainly suggest to the present minister that if the present system is as cumbersome as it appears to be, it should be changed. Either those in charge should be changed, or they should be instructed that the system must be improved so the representatives of the people may obtain the information which will place them in a position to judge how the affairs of the country are being run. That is particularly so with the members of the opposition, who are here for no other purpose than sought in the to be the critics of the government, the watchdogs of the treasury, on behalf of the people of Canada.

No. I take it that it is proper under this item to introduce a general question with regard to the organization of the department in respect of civilian employees. I was startled-I think it was a year ago-to find the large number of civilian employees. I think at that time
[Mr. Claxton.)

one was startled because of the relationship which they bore to the active army at that time. Since then of course the situation has changed very greatly. We have waked up more to the altered world situation, and our army has increased, and also our civilian employees have increased very largely. They constitute a tremendously large organization, and it was with regard to that that I wanted to ask the minister one or two questions, for I consider he has a tremendous job to organize in respect of both.
My understanding is, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, that there are some
30,000	civilian employees-these are rough figures-and that that represents an increase of some 5,000 within the last year. If I am approximately correct I will go on from there. My point is this. I wanted to ask the minister how that organization, which I call a very large one-perhaps the word "tremendous" would not be an exaggeration-is set up? What means has the minister taken to satisfy himself that this tremendously large body of men and women is organized to the best possible advantage, and in particular whether he is following the example that I think has been followed in at least one other department; whether he has availed himself of any outside assistance-what we may call expert assistance^-in the matter of organizing? Perhaps the minister would answer that question before I go any farther.

It is set up in accordance with the practice which has obtained in the Department of National Defence over the years. There has not been much change. We have to do a job, and we do it.
With reference to the numbers, they vary from time to time, in relation to the job we have to do. We have to secure the approval for the establishment of every position, the recommendation of the civil service commission, and that has to be approved by the treasury board. Teams of the civil service commission, the treasury board and representatives of the department and services have gone about to ascertain how many people we need to do each job in each place.
We have proportionately reduced the number of civil service employees in the department year after year since I came into the job, until last year. And now, with the expansion of the armed forces from the 1st of July, 1950, to the present date by almost 28,000, speaking from memory, that has naturally resulted in an increase in the number of civilians, because we feel civilians should do the jobs civilians can do. We anticipate a further substantial increase in the number of civilians, just as we anticipate

a further substantial increase in the number of service personnel. We think that is the best way to do it. Each job or group of jobs has to be approved by the civil service commission and treasury board, and filled through the ordinary government channels or, in the case of prevailing rate employees, through employment obtained usually through employment offices of the Department of Labour. I do not know what else the hon. member wants, in answer to the question.
He does not know.

I am sorry that apparently I have succeeded in making the minister feel that my question was a hostile one. It was not intended in that way. I assume we are here trying to look at these things as citizens regarding ourselves as more or less reasonable. This seems to me a matter of great importance which we might discuss on its merits.
Judging from his tone, apparently the minister resents my questions; but I hope that perhaps he will change his mind as we go along. He began by saying that, "We have a job and we do it," and that "We have always had an organization in the defence department," and, "We have developed as we have gone along." He has also said-and I applaud it-that they have the civil service commission and the treasury board teams to look after what they are doing, with a view to effecting economies, and trying to see that the number in the department is not greater than is necessary. That is all commendable.
Sure.

Yes; we are in agreement; thank you for your help. We all agree that is commendable; and I gather also that the minister, in spite of this very large task facing him, has not felt the need of availing himself of what I think ordinarily would be regarded as expert outside assistance. I would point out to the minister that I understand the film board which, I suppose, has perhaps only two or three per cent of the number of civilian employees in the defence department, did avail itself of a most reputable and respected organization which specializes in studies of efficiency.
I would be very interested to know why we would use it in a case where it would appear that efficiency ought to be much more easily scrutinized and ensured, as in the case of the film board, and would not care to use it here.

Would the hon. member suggest that an efficiency expert be called in
Supply-National Defence to say whether, for instance, army camps and airports, where cadets are in training, require hundreds of extra civilian help during the summertime? Would the hon. member suggest an expert to say how many cooks are required?

Let me make it clear that I am not suggesting that there are any experts I know of who should be called in to assist the Department of National Defence in dealing with troops. I am talking wholly about the civilian staff.
I am speaking about the civilians.

have thought it might be reasonable if an expert organization was brought in, yes, to find out how many civilians were needed to run a camp here or there. But when it comes to doing an over-all cutting job, then the only cutting knife there is is that of treasury board. And that has to be rough and tough; and that is done by my colleague the Minister of Finance. And what he has done in order to reduce the total number of civil servants outside the Department of National Defence has been quite amazing, in this time of national growth. I think I have impressed upon our department-because we are spending about three and a half times as much as all the other departments combined-that they have to be responsible to the utmost cent. And that is what I hope we will do.

I would suggest to the minister that the best, as judged by any standard, whether it be that of another nation or another department within our own. government service, does not necessarily mean that the job we are producing is the best that can be produced. I would ask the minister whether he would give serious consideration

Supply-National Defence to an examination of all these services, with a view to replacing men where possible with women, so as to release those men for active service.
In discussing this matter before the dinner hour it was suggested that there were many places in the. services where women could serve admirably so as to release men for active duty. I also say on behalf of the women that they will carry a great load- possibly greater than that now being carried.
Wherever possible that will be done.

It occurred to me, after having listened to the past several hours of discussion, that if the Kremlin had recording equipment in this building they would have considered by this time that any contemplated war they might start would be half won already.
The minister has been accused of giving broad and general answers to questions. But in all my experience here I have never listened to such a battery of broad and general statements and questions as I have heard during the past several hours. The whole thing is boring, as someone has asserted. I think it is boring particularly because there has been a complete absence of ability on the part of someone to sink his teeth into something concrete. It appears to me as though it might be the product of frustration.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Greenwood, and I would sum up what I heard him say, or what I thought I heard him say. He said, in effect, that something should be done, that something may be wrong-although he was not just sure what may be wrong. But something may be wrong, he thought, and therefore something should be done; and since he could not determine what was wrong-"Would you appoint an efficiency expert to tell me what is wrong, so that I can criticize?"
It is all right to talk about efficiency; we all desire to have it; but efficiency has taught us one thing, if nothing else, and that is that as a rule, and especially as applied to the armed services, where efficiency experts have been employed it has resulted in the immediate issue of a grand collection of new forms which are used for a short period of time, and then promptly forgotten-and, as the hon. member for Peace River suggests to me, as a rule they are put out, at the rate of twenty-five copies each.
I feel there are several extremely important issues relative to national defence that could be occupying our time profitably now; and that we should not have to listen to the

mere assertion that something may be wrong. I will criticize when I can find something wrong, something which I believe should be criticized. But I think we are not justified in repeating the simple assertion that something may be wrong-"We don't know what is wrong, but if you will tell us what is wrong, and let us determine how it is wrong, we will have something to criticize".
I am not questioning the right of anyone to adopt that course of action; but in my estimation when we have certain much more important issues before us including, I may say to my friends of the Progressive Conservative party, the whole manpower question, we should devote our time to a discussion of those questions, which are far more important than these simple issues to which we have been devoting the past several hours today and on previous occasions.
I suggest that in these grave times we would be well advised to get down to business and deal with certain of those factors which, to me, are of much greater importance at this extremely serious time. I doubt if anyone will deny that these are serious times.
I should like to ask a question of the hon. member who has just spoken, and who has so generously given us the benefit of his great experience-and he seems to have had vast experience-
Oh, oh.

-in the matter of efficiency experts dealing with military establishments. I should like to ask him the number of these, and if he would give us the benefit of his experience in that regard. He seems to have had a great deal of experience. He has said that in every case this or that has happened. Then, could we not be honoured or favoured by a further discourse in which he would set out specific instances where efficiency experts have caused less efficiency than before they started?
I would ask the hon. member to name some particular experiences where efficiency experts tried to do a job, and failed to do it.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I wonder if we are not getting away from the subject matter of the discussion.

speechtext: It is the subject of civil salaries and wages. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I have just ruled that the matter is closed.

I should like to ask the minister one question with regard to security. We are dealing with civilian employees of the Department of National Defence, and acting in their different capacities nearly all of them at one time or another will have access to material that is restricted, if not secret and top secret in character. What is the machinery for screening prospective employees who have to take the oath of secrecy under the Official Secrets Act? What percentage have taken this oath? What percentage of those who have been screened have taken the oath? I am not saying this in any spirit of criticism, but in view of what is going on in the world I do not think we can be too careful and we would like to know what is being done.
All of those who have access to top secret, secret or restricted information are screened before they have such access. All civil servants take the oath.
Is that the official secrets oath?
It is the oath of allegiance and, in some cases, of secrecy.
Does every civil servant, no matter what department or branch he is in, take the oath of secrecy?

It takes some time to get around to all of them, but that is done.

speechtext:

speechtext:

Let us get rid of it now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:

Taking them out.
From each item?

$4,303,500. Acquisition and construction of buildings and works, including acquisition of land, $350,000. All other expenditures other than special categories, $5,000, a total of $5,096,202.

$900,000 would not likely be spent.
$900,000 will not be spent?

Eighty.

$10,000, less of course what he gets as an army pensioner. As a major general having thirty-five years plus service I should think that he was working full time, and working very well, for about $3,500 a year.

from the minister's last statement that in the case of personnel of the Department of National Health and Welfare who are engaged in the work of civil defence, they will continue to be on the staff of his department and will draw their salaries as officials of that department, and not through the Department of National Defence?

Well, for instance, in my
judgment it is not necessary to create a special post or posts in the legal division, because the personnel in the legal division of the national health and welfare department have the time and ability to deal with legal matters. for Fraser Valley will appreciate that when a minister replies he requires perhaps more latitude in order to give a full explanation than hon. members would be allowed in putting their questions. On a point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Both hon. members will please take their seats. I think we must continue with the discussion of this item covering civil salaries and wages. speechtext: I most certainly can answer it, and I think I have answered it. I have said there are now twenty-seven posts. There was a plan for sixty additional posts. Supply-National Defence of building up a big staff which is not necessary. Are we to take the minister's last statement to indicate his present view that none of the additional sixty are likely to be required?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I cannot say more than I have said for the time being.

I would humbly suggest that it would be much better for us to take up at one time all the questions we are going to ask with regard to civil defence and get them out of the way. I think that procedure would expedite matters considerably. Whether we do it now or whether we do it at a later time, I do not care. But I would suggest that it could all be done at the same time instead of being scattered all through the estimates of the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
As he knows, the civil defence co-ordinator is a distinguished soldier and a man who has, with regard to a very difficult task, admittedly done a very good job as civil defence co-ordinator in this country, as will be reflected in the opinion which I know every minister in each of our provinces responsible for civilian defence would vouchsafe to give.
The job of the civil defence co-ordinator in principle is the same as that of his predecessors, of whom Dr. Manion, a former leader of the opposition, was a very distinguished one. The job consists, under ministerial authority, responsible to the government as a whole, in establishing liaison with those groups, such as the provincial governments, who are responsible for their creatures the municipalities, and in establishing relationships with them in trying to bring about a policy of co-ordination in respect of civil defence.
Hon. gentlemen will remember what I said in my opening statement, that the federal government, in the pursuit of this problem, does not feel that it is possible to provide at the centre, on an operational level, a full effective measure of civil defence. We -have certain functions, the function of getting out training manuals, of publications, all of which come under the civil defence co-ordinator, the use of films, the purchase of equipment of various kinds, which we are prepared to give to the civil defence directors and workers who operate under the provinces or under the municipalities-generally we have the role of co-ordination.
But one should not judge the adequacy of civil defence in this country only by the recital of policy, or the recital of achievement of the federal government; for we cannot do this job alone, as I said quite frankly the other day. If one is going to provide for a measure of adequate civil defence it has to be done through a policy of decentralization, through the provinces and through the municipalities, which must carry on the primary responsibility of an operational endeavour.
I am happy to be able to say that as a result of the work of the civil defence co-ordinator, who has worked tirelessly during the last year and a half, every city in Canada but one, of 50,000 and over, has a civil defence director. These directors are paid by the


municipality, and the civil defence co-ordinator of this country has been largely responsible for stimulating action by way of appointments in so many of these municipalities.
One of his first jobs of course was to establish contact with the United Kingdom civil defence authorities. It was the civil defence co-ordinator who made all the detailed preliminary arrangements for the agreement that we were able to arrive at with the United States in respect of a policy of common civil defence, so that we could say that for purposes of civil defence there would be no border.
It is the function of the civil defence co-ordinator to continue contacts with these various bodies. To give an example, the other day in Sault Ste. Marie-this is a point of some interest in this connection-the minister in charge, the Hon. Mr. Welsh, telephoned me and asked me if the services of the civil defence co-ordinator could be used to deal with a problem that had arisen in connection with a civil defence matter in Sault Ste. Marie. The civil defence co-ordinator was dispatched there. This morning I had a letter from Colonel Welsh commenting upon the value of these services and other matters.
A month ago the civil defence co-ordinator went to the province of British Columbia, to deal with the government of that province.
He had a task there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
He met with the officials of the city of Vancouver as well in connection with his task.
The civil defence co-ordinator was responsible for the three schools that we had during the course of the winter, as a result of which we have trained over 200 people, who in turn have gone back to their municipalities to take on local civil defence direction jobs, or perform some function or other in that particular.
It was the civil defence co-ordinator who organized the present school that is under way at Connaught Ranges. I have just given a general survey which I know my hon. friend will appreciate. I may say that General Worthington has a very full job, and I want to say what I said at the beginning; he is doing that job admirably.

I doubt whether there are
many people in this country who are more familiar with the integrity, industry and the great ability of General Worthington than I am. I am going on record to say that never has a public servant in this land been asked to make bricks with less straw than General Worthington is being asked to do

today. I say that out of a total of almost $2 billion to be spent on defence we are spending now the small sum of about $4 million for the whole of civil defence. I repeat what 1 said a few moments ago; I believe this country will be stunned when it realizes what a paltry effort is being made in this direction.
The minister has told us some of the functions. You have instructors; you have a school at Connaught. Films are to be purchased. Then there is some suggestion of linking in with the medical officers in the department looking after Indians to help out. The big function which has to be faced today as far as civil defence is concerned is that of establishing a warning system, and there is no warning system whatever in this country at the present time. I believe no results have been achieved in so far as co-ordinating a plan for a warning system with United States-

Yes, that is right.

He did not.

speechtext:

speechtext:
My hon. friend says to go

May I make this comment as
to the difficulty which would be raised if we try to make too fine a distinction as to what may or may not be asked in connection with [DOT] wages and salaries. This is a very important subject which, for reasons which I do not think anyone is criticizing, does not appear as a segregated item in the estimates of the Department of National Defence. It is wrapped up in a number of other items all contained within the bracket of departmental administration. It is perfectly true that the amount that would be set aside for the physical material, including such things as warning systems and things of that kind, would not come in under the first line, it would be included somewhere down below-although we do not know where.
It seems to me that where we have a wrapped-up package like this, we shall get along faster and further if we carry forward with the idea the minister seemed ready to accept, namely that this be opened up for discussion and that we do not try to put it into airtight compartments. [The Deputy Chairman.]

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is a lot of good in the suggestion of the leader of the opposition. But would it not be proper to apply the same principle to this item for departmental administration, in the Department of National Defence? If we take them in bulk, and have a discussion on each item at random, without just limiting ourselves to civil salaries and wages, could we not apply that good principle to the whole department, and thus take up the item of $13,419,162- because this afternoon, although we were on the first item of civil salaries and .wages, most of the time was spent in a discussion of other details' which go to make up this total sum of $13,419,162. As the minister has directed his remarks to what I have just said, I should like to point out the very great difference. The point I make is that because this is a new branch of activity in the department, and because it does not appear under any separate item, the minister might now deal with it. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
May I ask the

Supply-National Defence

Mr. Chairman, may I remind you what did take place. As distinguished

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I said plus other figures.

If that disposes of the review of civil defence at this stage, recognizing the item will of course come up again at a later point when it is called-

Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I agree with what my hon. friend is saying. At a quarter to ten that is the very thing I wanted to do acting upon the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary East, and I now propose to follow that course. As my hon. friend will note, the transfer of responsibilities from the Minister of National Defence to the Department of National Health and Welfare took place at a time after the estimates of the Department of National Defence had been formulated.
I know that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That explains why we are operating in this quasi-dual position at the moment.
Jumbled position.

The civil defence estimates, broken down by the usual primaries, are shown as my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence has indicated, and as I suggested the other night. Anticipated expenditures for the present year total $4,196,202. Because of the necessity of placing orders now for equipment or materials and supplies which will not actually be delivered or paid for until 1952 or 1953, authority is also being asked for permission to enter into commitments against funds for 1952-53 totalling $900,000, and against funds for 1953-44 totalling $1,822,500. Nor does it include the very significant sums of money that are being' spent by the provinces. Nor does it include the significant sums that are being spent by the municipalities. The hon. member for Nanaimo in making his criticism, quite properly from his point of view, said that he thought that the figure which had been given for civil 

defence in Canada was an unsatisfactory one. I can only say that if he will compare that figure with the figures now proposed in the United States for civil defence, and with the figures proposed and budgeted for in the United Kingdom for civil defence at the present time, he will find that we are by no means lagging behind in financial commitments for this purpose.
