speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I will give the whole picture now that the question has been asked. I do not believe it is fair to the people of Canada to suggest that the determination of an adequate civil defence program represents the mere expenditure of dollars and cents. The only proper way in the long run to really provide for adequate civil defence in Canada is by recognition of the principle of mutual aid at the closest operational level, the municipality. That sort of thing is incalculable. If anyone thinks we are going to have an adequate civil defence program just by the expenditure of money, I would take strong issue with that point of view. All over this country organizations are developing composed of men and women many of whom are devoting a great deal of their leisure time to this work without any thought of reward or compensation. If it were possible to total all work of that kind the figure would certainly be much more impressive than it seems at first glance. I also want to say that if I came before this house with a figure on federal account that as much larger than the figure I have indicated, I know what hon. gentlemen opposite would say. They would criticize us for the unnecessary expenditure of money in a field where private voluntary effort can do so much.
These figures have been gone over with the provinces, with whom we had a meeting on February 23 under the chairmanship of my colleague the Minister of National Defence. At that meeting there was a very wide measure of agreement. Only last Friday I conferred with the minister responsible for civil defence in our largest and most thickly populated province, and I can say he and I are fully agreed on the common plans we are each pursuing. He knows the expenditures we are making; and while I would not go so far as to say he agreed with everything, I know he and I see eye to eye on this important matter. Tomorrow I am having a conference with the minister of welfare of Saskatchewan, who is in charge of civil defence for that province. While he thinks we should assume certain responsibilities in connection with their training schools, when we outline the division of responsibilities as

between the province and the dominion I am sure I would not do him an injustice if I said I am sure he would generally concur in the position we have taken.
The project we have in mind may be grouped under five general headings: purchase of equipment, purchase of material and supplies, construction of technical training schools, production of training aid pamphlets, and so on. Under the purchase of equipment $2,441,500 is being asked to cover expenditures this year, with an additional $650,000 commitment authority against 1952-53 funds and $1,072,500 against 1953-54 funds. That is subject to change depending upon the assessment we get from the only authoritative source, the chiefs of staff. The program can be accelerated, depending upon that advice. I am certain that as long as I am in charge of this difficult assignment I am not going to go ahead and build up an organization which in the event of disuse would rust and do more harm than good. I believe it is the feeling of those in charge of this work that we should be in a position to act in the light of the assessment we get as to probabilities, as to the state of international tension, and so on. We may make a big miscalculation; there can be no doubt of that possibility, but certain risks have to be taken in this matter. Those risks have to be borne not only by the armed forces but by everyone in Canada, for that is the nature of total war, and no minister of the crown or anyone else can alter that unfortunate fact.
The largest expenditure under this item is for fire-fighting equipment. We propose to spend $977,500 for such equipment this year. Actually we are now concluding an arrangement with the province of Ontario in respect of which we have signified our willingness and intention to provide something in the neighbourhood of $300,000, depending upon the presentation of details, to assist them in a program of standardization of hose couplings. That is a very important item in civil defence work, for the disaster that comes through fire is one of the most important considerations to be borne in mind. An amount of $300,000 in addition may be committed against next year's funds and $697,500 against the 1953-54 funds under the program of standardization of hose couplings; but that, too, depends on the ability of the fire chiefs and those in the provinces in charge of fire work generally to bring about a common standard in the use of hose couplings. We estimate that under this item $900,000 will be spent this year on this phase of the program. From conversations I have had with Sir John Hodsoll, the director of civil defence in Britain, and
Supply-National Defence with Governor Caldwell, his opposite number in the United States, that is an expenditure which in the light of their experience they regard as fundamental, and one of the initial expenditures that should be undertaken.
Another large item under this heading is radiation detection instruments, for which $962,000 will be spent this year with an additional $50,000 being ordered but paid for next year. The sum of $550,000 is required, we estimate, for medical equipment, $100,000 to be actually spent this year and orders placed for an additional $450,000 worth of equipment, approximately half of which will be delivered and paid for next year and the remaining half possibly in the ensuing year. That, too, is subject to acceleration, depending upon the appraisal we get from the responsible military authorities.
Other items being purchased and paid for this year under this heading are: sirens, $252,000; special rescue equipment, $35,000; certain vehicles, $45,000; training equipment, $10,000; communications equipment, $20,000.
That last item has an important relationship to the question put by the hon. member for Nanaimo as to the warning system, and I may as well deal with his question now. In connection with the warning system the plan is that we will be responsible for the warning to the municipality, but from then on the municipality will have to act in the light of that warning. I would not want to say the warning system is complete. It is by no means complete, but we are developing that system just as quickly as it is possible to do so.
Since April 1 orders have actually been placed for the following equipment: 70 radiation detection instruments, $11,515;	1,300
stirrup pumps at a cost of from $1.50 to $3.50 each, totalling $3,300;	10,000 steel
helmets at 80 cents each, $8,000; stretchers, $1,400; 500 suits of protective clothing, $1,750.
Did the radiation equipment total $11,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I gave the total as $962,000 to be spent this year.
Mr. Cold well: For what municipality are the stretchers being bought for which $1,400 is being paid?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend is not going to suggest by that good-humoured question that this is an attempt to provide stretchers for the whole country. He knows that is not the case.
What is it for, then?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It is for the training centres. If my hon. friend would come out with me tomorrow to the school at Connaught Ranges

Supply-National Defence he would see why we must have some stretchers available. Some of these stretchers will also be used at the school in Saskatchewan, at the school that is going to be established in British Columbia, and at the schools that are to be established in two other provinces. As to the equipment in the municipality, that will be provided by the municipality in accordance with arrangements made by the provinces following action to be taken by the Canadian Red Cross Society, and with the assistance that will be provided by the St. John Ambulance Corps, which are taking a great share of the load in the business of first aid training.

Will the minister give the
figures on steel helmets again?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: At how much?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Ten thousand steel helmets
at 80 cents each. We are getting them at a bargain price. Now I will deal with the purchase of other material and supplies. $800,000 is requested to cover this year's expenditures on materials and supplies with an additional $250,000 commitment against next year's funds and a further three-quarters of a million-dollar commitment against 1953-54 funds.
The largest item under this heading is for clothing civil defence volunteers; approximately $400,000 is required this year and an additional $500,000 to be committed against 1953-54 funds.
To meet the cost of necessary stockpiling of medical supplies, to be carried out in conjunction with the armed services program, will require an expenditure this year of $250,000, with an additional $250,000 worth to be ordered this year and paid for out of future funds when deliveries can actually be made.
I hope I am not going into too much detail.
Not enough.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
But rather than be criticized
for not giving enough, I propose to give the detail in extenso.
The sum of $75,000 will also be spent this year on the purchase of respirators with an additional $250,000 worth being ordered and paid for next year when deliveries can actually be made.
Other items under this heading, to be purchased and paid for this year, are:
Protective clothing, $10,000.
Gasoline, oil and lubricants, $4,000.
Catering for training school, $62,500.
On the production of training aids and pamphlets there will be spent this year $51,500 in accordance with the plans that we


have had as a result of our discussions with the provinces who regard that-and I think properly so for the most part-as our responsibility. In addition to the pamphlets that we are preparing, we will also have the use of pamphlets which have been prepared in the United Kingdom and in the United States and which have been re-adapted for use in this country.
We expect that $25,000 will be spent this year on the purchase of certain civil defence films. Two of them have actually been purchased and are being used for educational purposes. These films are not intended to provoke undue fear and panic but rather to indicate the kind of precautionary measures that can be taken by the civilian population in the event of the kind of disaster which none of us wishes to see happen.
Those figures will give an idea of the expenditures we propose to make this year. I can well understand the argument that might be made that this is not enough. All I can say is that in the light of the organization as it exists, in the light of the arrangements we have made with the provinces, and with the assumption by the municipalities all over this country of the responsibility that they are now assuming, we feel that this represents the wisest expenditure at this time. I can only say that a situation could arise whereby there would be an acceleration of that program, but that would depend on other non-existing circumstances.
I do not want to repeat the general outlines of our policy as given in my earlier statement. It seems to me that those principles will commend themselves to most reasonable people in this country. They represent a recognition of the federal character of this country, and of the impossibility of the central authority doing this job fully. The job is one for the provinces. It is one that must be carried on primarily in each municipality. The basis of the civil defence organization will be the voluntary effort that will be put into this matter, by the Canadian people. I can only say that, in the light of the situation as we see it, we will do everything that we can to give, in co-operation with the other two levels of government, a civil defence program as adequate as it is possible to give. From my contacts with authorities in the United States and with Sir John Hodsoll, the civil defence director in the United Kingdom, I have reason to believe that we are proceeding on sound lines.

I was most interested in
listening to the minister's explanation and tO' the detailed information he has given with regard to the expenditures we are making

for civil defence. In particular he mentioned approximately $900,000 for the purchase of fire-extinguishing apparatus.
Hose couplings.

Yes, hose couplings. Suppose that there is a former soldier or officer who is put in charge of civil defence in any locality, and he wants to organize the protection of his municipality in case of an enemy attack. He may rely on the goodwill of the people of his community. Then I understand that the first thing he will have to do will toe to get in touch with the provincial minister who is supposed to be the contact man for the organization of civil defence. Is that right?
That is correct.

With regard to the amount, whatever it is, that is spent toy Ottawa for civil defence-$900,000 approximately for hose couplings, and all that-I understand that it will be given by Ottawa to the provinces; will it toe given by Ottawa to the various bigger municipalities such as Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver or Winnipeg, or will it
Supply-National Defence be given to the provincial authorities? It is nearly eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman-
It is past eleven.
I hope that the minister will be kind enough to give the information when the committee meets again.

I will do that with great pleasure.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
